config.title: Minimum Window Substring

intro.title: Minimum Window Substring
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds the smallest substring in a given string that contains all characters of another target string. You will learn the core concept of the sliding window technique, which efficiently expands and contracts a window over the string to find the minimum valid substring. The main technologies involved are JavaScript strings, objects for frequency counting, and loops to traverse the string. This beginner-friendly approach will help you understand how to solve complex string lessons with optimized two-pointer logic.
intro.usecase: The Minimum Window Substring algorithm powers intelligent search and filtering features in modern applications. When you type in a search bar within a large document editor or codebase, this algorithm helps find the smallest relevant snippet containing all your search terms. It's also used in data analysis dashboards to identify the most concise data segment matching multiple filter criteria, and in DNA sequence analysis tools to locate the shortest genetic segment containing specific marker patterns. As a developer, you'll implement this pattern when building efficient text search, data mining, or content recommendation features.

objectives: Implement a sliding window algorithm to find substrings
Construct character frequency maps for pattern matching
Manipulate window boundaries to expand and contract the search range
Initialize and update counters to track required characters
Apply conditional logic to validate when a window contains all target characters
Configure loop structures to iterate through the input string efficiently
Integrate comparison operations to identify the minimum valid window

content.body: Have you ever needed to find the smallest piece of text that contains all the letters you're looking for? In this lesson, we'll learn the Minimum Window Substring algorithm. You'll discover how to efficiently find the shortest substring that contains all target characters using a clever moving window technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
1. Explain what a sliding window represents in string lessons
2. Apply the expand-and-shrink logic to find minimum windows
3. Implement the Minimum Window Substring algorithm in JavaScript
4. Identify when to expand versus shrink the window during execution
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a small example. Look at this string: 'ADOBECODEBANC'. We want to find the shortest continuous piece that contains all the letters 'A', 'B', and 'C'. What's the smallest segment you can find that includes A, B, and C? Try to identify it visually.
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now imagine you're highlighting a segment of the string that starts at the first 'A'. As you move the right end of your highlight further right, you collect more letters. When should you stop expanding to the right? When should you start moving the left end forward instead?
content.title: Think about movement

content.body: You just explored the string by considering different segments. You probably started with a small window and expanded it, or maybe you tried different starting points. This intuitive checking of various segments is similar to what we'll systematize.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Manually checking every possible substring in a long string becomes impractical. For a string of length 1000, there are over 500,000 possible substrings to check! We need a method that moves through the string just once, intelligently adjusting our window.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Think of a moving segment or window that slides across the string. The window expands to include more characters when we haven't found all our target letters yet. It shrinks from the left when we have all the letters, trying to find the smallest valid window. This expand-and-shrink dance is the sliding window pattern.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Highlight a moving segment of the array; show expand and shrink.

content.body: We'll use two pointers (left and right) to represent our window edges. We expand the window by moving the right pointer forward, collecting characters. When we have all required characters, we try to shrink from the left while still keeping all required characters. We track the smallest valid window we find.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize left and right pointers at the start
2. Expand the window by moving right pointer, counting characters
3. When we have all required characters, record the window size
4. Try to shrink from the left while still having all characters
5. Repeat steps 2-4 until we've processed the entire string
6. Return the smallest valid window found
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function and variables
steps.instruction: Create the function skeleton and initialize the main variables we'll need. We'll need left and right pointers, character count maps, and tracking variables.
steps.hint: Start with function minWindow(s, t) and declare let variables for left, right, and result tracking.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have the function signature correct.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's begin with the basic function structure: function minWindow(s, t) {}

steps.title: Initialize pointers and tracking variables
steps.instruction: Add the variables we need: left and right pointers, character count maps for what we need and what we have, and variables to track matches and the result.
steps.hint: Create let left = 0, right = 0, needMap = new Map(), haveMap = new Map(), and variables for match tracking.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Check that you have all the variables: pointers, maps, and result tracker.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need left, right pointers, maps for needed/have counts, and result tracking.

steps.title: Populate the need map
steps.instruction: Before we start sliding, we need to know what characters we're looking for. Fill the needMap with counts of each character in string t.
steps.hint: Loop through t and update needMap with character counts. Also set need = needMap.size.
steps.expectedOutcome: needMap filled with target character counts
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're counting characters correctly and setting need to the map size.
steps.feedbackWrong: Loop through t and count each character into needMap, then set need = needMap.size.

steps.title: Implement the main sliding window loop
steps.instruction: Add the while loop that moves the right pointer through the string. Inside, update haveMap with the current character and check if we've matched needed counts.
steps.hint: while (right < s.length) { update haveMap for s[right]; check character matches; right++ }
steps.expectedOutcome: Right pointer moves through string, updating counts
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good structure. Make sure you're updating have when a character count matches exactly what's needed.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to move right through the string, update haveMap, and check when character counts match needMap.

steps.title: Add the shrink logic
steps.instruction: When we have all required characters (have === need), we try to shrink from the left. Add this logic inside the main loop after the expansion.
steps.hint: while (have === need) { update result if current window is smaller; remove left char from haveMap; if it breaks a match, decrement have; left++ }
steps.expectedOutcome: Window shrinks when all characters are found
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Make sure you're updating result when finding smaller windows and properly adjusting have when shrinking.
steps.feedbackWrong: When have === need, try to shrink: update result if window smaller, remove left char, adjust have if needed, move left pointer.

steps.title: Add the return statement
steps.instruction: After the loop completes, check if we found a valid window and return the appropriate substring or empty string.
steps.hint: If result[1] is still Infinity, return empty string. Otherwise, return s.slice(result[0], result[1] + 1).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. Make sure you handle the case where no valid window was found.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check if result[1] is still Infinity (no window found) and return appropriate substring.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented the Minimum Window Substring algorithm using the sliding window pattern. Remember: the window expands when we need more characters and shrinks when we have all required characters, always tracking the smallest valid window. This pattern is powerful for many substring and subarray lessons where you need to find contiguous segments meeting certain criteria.
